slides.title: Stage-1 Calibration: Procurement and Build
slides.subtitle: The spheres, board and fixtures needed for the depth-sensor calibration captures
slides.notes: This is the first of two decks on the stage-1 calibration captures. It covers what has to be bought and made before a capture session: two matte spheres, a flat board, their mountings on the robot flange, and a three-ball nest, with estimated costs and candidate suppliers. The second deck covers the test procedure itself and what the robot program must do. Both are summaries of the stage-1 capture procedure in docs/procedures, whose section 3a and appendix A hold the full build details.

slides.title: Two spheres and a board carry the known geometry
slides.caption: Sphere on its stem, side view: the stem points away from the sensor so that the sphere hides it.

cards.head: Sphere A
cards.text: 76.2 mm diameter; used from 300 to 550 mm

cards.head: Sphere B
cards.text: 152.4 mm diameter; used from 500 to 1,100 mm

cards.head: Board
cards.text: 200 x 150 mm, at least 6 mm thick, flat to 0.05 mm after painting; tilted 0, 20 and 40 degrees

slides.notes: The calibration compares what the sensor measures with targets of known shape held at known poses by the robot. Two sphere sizes are used because the bias from averaging over a curved surface depends on curvature; two radii a factor of two apart let the correction map carry curvature as an input and remove that bias. Both spheres are used around 500 to 550 mm so the two radii overlap. The board supplies zero curvature and controlled tilts. A sphere's orientation does not matter, only its center, which is why the mounting must hold the center fixed rather than aim the sphere precisely.

slides.title: What must be built

rows: Sphere-flange mounts: adapter plates and stems
Run-out fixture: dial indicator on a magnetic base and steel base plate

slides.caption: Section 1b of the procedure; nothing outside sections 1a to 1f is needed for a session.
slides.notes: This is the complete list of apparatus to build before the first session, as section 1b of the procedure gives it. The dimensioned shop drawings are in appendix D of the stage-1 procedure, and as PNG files in docs/procedures/drawings/ of the repository: SC1-01 and SC1-02 adapter plates, SC1-03 and SC1-04 stems with the sphere interfaces, SC1-05 board adapter, SC1-06 nest base. The rigid sensor mount is built from the existing drawing from previous work. The run-out fixture needs no drawing: it is a bought dial indicator on a bought magnetic base, standing on a plain steel plate bolted to the table. Everything already in hand, everything to buy and the preparation tasks are on the following slides and in sections 1a, 1c and 1f.

slides.title: What must be bought

rows: Outside micrometers 75-100 and 150-175 mm, with setting standards
Rough TCP length; board distance D
Thread locker, retaining compound, shims, alcohol, padded cases

slides.caption: A phone camera is enough for the setup photos. Already in hand: sensor, robot, capture computer with its communication software, analysis computer.
slides.notes: These are the tools and consumables, section 1c of the procedure. The two outside micrometers replace any laboratory measurement: the sphere diameters are measured in-house after the matte finish, at six or more orientations, and the spread of the readings doubles as the sphericity check. The micrometers come with setting standards, which are used to check them before each measurement. The straightedge with a 0.05 mm feeler leaf checks the board's flatness after painting and after mounting. Items already in hand are the sensor, the robot, the capture computer with its communication software, which also takes the capture trigger from the robot, and the analysis computer.

slides.title: Building and buying cost about $2,525 to $6,500

rows: Sphere-flange mounts: two adapter plates and two stems
Run-out fixture: dial indicator, magnetic base, steel base plate

stats.label: bearing-ball sphere A, aluminum sphere B, tools included
both spheres made to order, tools included

slides.caption: Tools and consumables $685 to $1,430, included in the totals. Estimates of October 2026, plus or minus 50 percent; sphere B is the least certain.
slides.notes: These estimates come from suppliers' list prices where they exist and from typical job-shop rates of about 80 to 150 dollars an hour otherwise. The sphere figures no longer include a laboratory measurement: the diameters are measured in-house with the micrometers on the buy list. The two totals differ only in the spheres: a bearing ball with a bonded stem and a turned aluminum sphere, against both spheres made to order by a ball or ceramics maker. The rigid sensor mount is built from an existing drawing and is not estimated here. Quotes are needed before ordering, and the sphere choice is still to be settled after a canvass of the market.

slides.title: Purchase specification: target spheres

rows: Known to 0.025 mm, by micrometer at six or more orientations after finishing
Same; measure at the session's room temperature
Bearing-grade steel (52100 or 440C, grade 25 or better) or ceramic
Turned aluminum (6061-T6), solid or hollow with 6 mm wall
Matte, light, uniform: fine glass-bead blast or thin matte paint
Matte hard anodize, same appearance as sphere A
Steel: blind hole 10 H7 x 23 mm, stem bonded. Ceramic: maker's M8 insert
M20 x 30 mm tapped hole at a pole, 32 mm spot face

slides.caption: Procedure section 1d; drawings SC1-03 and SC1-04 show the interfaces.
slides.notes: This is the purchase specification of section 1d of the procedure, to hand to a supplier or a machine shop. The diameter requirement is decision D-13: known to 0.025 mm after the matte finish, measured in-house with the outside micrometers; the mean of six or more readings goes in the pose log, and their spread checks the 0.02 mm sphericity. Aluminum grows 0.0035 mm in diameter per degree C at sphere B's size, so it is measured at the temperature of the session. The dimensioned shop drawings are in appendix D of the stage-1 procedure, and as PNG files in docs/procedures/drawings/ of the repository: SC1-01 and SC1-02 adapter plates, SC1-03 and SC1-04 stems with the sphere interfaces, SC1-05 board adapter, SC1-06 nest base.

slides.title: Purchase specification: flat plate

rows: 200 x 150 mm, at least 6 mm thick
Finish-ground aluminum tooling plate (for example MIC-6) or float glass
0.05 mm over the front face, checked with a straightedge and a 0.05 mm feeler leaf after painting and after mounting
Thin, even matte light-gray paint; do not bead-blast a plate thinner than about 10 mm
Bottom long edge and left short edge square and clean: they rest on the adapter's edge pins
Supplier's flatness report, kept with the session notes

slides.caption: Procedure section 1d; the board outline is on drawing SC1-05.
slides.notes: The board is checked flat after painting and after mounting because that is the state the sensor sees, and the flatness report is the reference for the board-flatness check in the validation. A 6 mm plate sags only about 0.002 mm under its own weight, so thickness is a matter of surviving the finish and the mounting, not stiffness. The bottom and left edges locate the board against the three edge pins of the board adapter, which centers it on the flange axis. The dimensioned shop drawings are in appendix D of the stage-1 procedure, and as PNG files in docs/procedures/drawings/ of the repository: SC1-01 and SC1-02 adapter plates, SC1-03 and SC1-04 stems with the sphere interfaces, SC1-05 board adapter, SC1-06 nest base.

slides.title: Spheres must be matte and measured, not certified

columns.head: Finish
points: Every bearing ball arrives mirror-bright: unusable
Bead-blast with fine glass bead: removes micrometers
Matte paint is second choice: 0.02 to 0.05 mm per coat
"Chrome steel" is the 52100 alloy, not plating

columns.head: Diameter
points: Known to 0.025 mm, measured after the finish
Measured in-house by outside micrometer at six or more orientations
Aluminum grows 0.0035 mm per degree C: measure at session temperature
The mean goes in the pose log; the spread checks sphericity

columns.head: Mounting
points: Hardened balls cannot be tapped
Steel ball: drilled or EDM blind hole, bonded stem
Aluminum sphere B: thread cut when it is turned
No pre-tapped precision sphere exists above 1.5 inch

slides.notes: A mirror finish returns one bright highlight from the sensor's projector and almost nothing else, so every sphere must be made matte. Bead-blasting is preferred because it changes the diameter by only micrometers. The diameter requirement is decision D-13: known to 0.025 mm after finishing, which is a radius error of about 0.0125 mm, an eighth of the target at 500 mm; no maker's certificate is needed. The diameter is measured in-house with the outside micrometers; EDM means electrical discharge machining. Bearing-grade balls are hardened to about 60 HRC and cannot be tapped afterwards, which is why steel spheres get a bonded stem.

rows: Bal-tec; RGP Balls; Industrial Tectonics; Morgan Advanced Materials

MetrologyWorks up to 1.5 inch; Rothbucher 145 mm, sphericity 0.3 mm

Painted matte after grinding; flatness checked after mounting
Local machine shop; EDM shop for hardened balls
Outside micrometers: Mitutoyo 103-140-10 and 103-143-10, or Starrett
In-house, after the matte finish; setting standards included
Mitutoyo 2046 series; Noga MG71003 or DG-61003

slides.caption: From suppliers' web pages, October 2026; not an endorsement. Confirm size, finish, measurement and thread before ordering.
slides.notes: This list is appendix A of the procedure in brief. No supplier was found that stocks a precision sphere of the needed sizes with a mounting hole, so the spheres are either made to order or built from a bearing ball by a machine shop. The laser-scanner reference spheres sold in the right sizes generally have form errors of 0.5 to 2 mm, far too coarse; the Rothbucher sphere is the best specified of them. The finished diameters are measured in-house with outside micrometers, which is cheaper than buying certified spheres and is what the calibration actually needs.

slides.title: Run-out fixture: dial indicator and its mounting

cards.head: Dial indicator
cards.text: 0.01 mm graduation, about 10 mm travel; for example Mitutoyo 2046 series, about $50 to $150

cards.head: Magnetic base
cards.text: Articulating, with fine adjustment; for example Noga MG71003 or DG-61003, about $140 to $320

cards.head: Steel base plate
cards.text: About 150 x 100 x 12 mm, bolted to the cell table with two M8 screws, so the base holds on any table and does not creep

cards.head: Placement
cards.text: Where the indicator tip reaches the board's front face about 20 mm from an edge with the robot in its run-out pose

slides.caption: The run-out check: the flange turns, the indicator stays still, the reading must stay within 0.05 mm.
slides.notes: The run-out check in deck 2 needs the dial indicator held still while the robot turns the board about the flange axis. A magnetic base alone can creep or fail to hold on an aluminum or stone table, so it stands on a small steel plate bolted to the table. All three items are stocked by McMaster-Carr and the usual tool suppliers. The fixture needs no drawing beyond the plate's size and its two bolt holes.

slides.title: A stiff, repeatable chain from flange to sphere
slides.caption: Adapter on the flange's dowel, with the stem's shoulder seated on the adapter face.
points: Adapter located by the flange dowel, so a remount lands in the same place
Ground stem, 16 mm for A and 30 mm for B, keeps sag to 0.02 to 0.05 mm
Stem length at least 2R + 50 mm, so the sphere hides the stem
Witness mark across stem and adapter shows a loosened joint
After any remount, re-check in the nest: readings within 0.1 mm
slides.notes: Where the sphere center ends up does not need to be known from drawings, because the tool-center-point routine measures it; what matters is that it does not move afterwards. The adapter plate's mounting face, outer face and tapped hole are machined in one lathe setup, located on the flange pilot, so the hole is perpendicular to the face within 0.02 mm over 100 mm. The stems are deliberately thick: a 12 mm stem would let sphere A sag about 0.07 mm, and that sag would change with the robot's orientation. The shoulder on the stem, machined square in the same setup as its thread, sets the stem perpendicular to the adapter. The dimensioned shop drawings are in appendix D of the stage-1 procedure, and as PNG files in docs/procedures/drawings/ of the repository: SC1-01 and SC1-02 adapter plates, SC1-03 and SC1-04 stems with the sphere interfaces, SC1-05 board adapter, SC1-06 nest base. The adapter plates are 63 mm across, 16 mm thick for sphere A and 22 mm for sphere B, with a 31.5 mm centering spigot and one 6 mm dowel for the ISO 9409-1-50-4-M6 flange.

slides.title: The sphere end: threaded insert or bonded stem
slides.label: Ceramic sphere: maker's threaded insert
slides.caption: The hole need not be exactly radial: the tool-center-point routine measures the center wherever it ends up.
slides.notes: Precision ceramic spheres are sold with a threaded insert bonded in by the maker; the stem tip is turned to a matching thread with a small shoulder that seats on the flat around the insert, with a drop of medium-strength thread locker. Bearing-grade steel balls are hardened to about 60 HRC and cannot be tapped, so a shop makes a blind hole about 0.6 R deep by carbide drilling or electrical discharge machining, sized for a light press fit, and the stem is bonded in with anaerobic retaining compound. Never weld or braze: the heat distorts the sphere. A turned aluminum sphere B can have the stem thread cut into it when it is made. The dimensioned shop drawings are in appendix D of the stage-1 procedure, and as PNG files in docs/procedures/drawings/ of the repository: SC1-01 and SC1-02 adapter plates, SC1-03 and SC1-04 stems with the sphere interfaces, SC1-05 board adapter, SC1-06 nest base.

slides.title: The board must stay flat after finishing and mounting
slides.caption: Board on its adapter. The runout and frame checks shown here are done at setup (deck 2).

cards.head: Plate
cards.text: 200 x 150 mm, at least 6 mm thick; ground aluminum tooling plate or float glass

cards.head: Finish
cards.text: Matte light gray paint on the front face; do not bead-blast a plate thinner than about 10 mm, it bows

cards.head: Flatness
cards.text: 0.05 mm, checked after painting and mounting, not before; keep the flatness report

cards.head: Adapter
cards.text: Three support pads, three edge pins and three clamp fingers hold the board square to the flange axis, centered on it, and in the same place after a remount

slides.notes: Thickness is not a stiffness question: a 6 mm plate sags only about 0.002 mm under its own weight. It only has to survive the finish and the mounting flat. Bead-blasting peens one face and bows a thin plate, so paint over the ground or glass surface instead. Flatness is checked last, after painting and mounting, because that is the state the sensor sees; the flatness report is also the reference for the board-flatness check in the validation. The dimensioned shop drawings are in appendix D of the stage-1 procedure, and as PNG files in docs/procedures/drawings/ of the repository: SC1-01 and SC1-02 adapter plates, SC1-03 and SC1-04 stems with the sphere interfaces, SC1-05 board adapter, SC1-06 nest base.

slides.title: A three-ball nest holds each sphere at a fixed center
points: Three hardened balls, 24 mm diameter, bonded into pockets on a 60 mm circle in a 120 mm steel base
Ordinary grade-25 bearing balls are good enough: the nest's quality comes from the balls being rigidly fixed
Bolted to the table where the robot reaches with the wrist down and tilted about 40 degrees to either side
Used once per sphere at setup, and after any remount of an adapter or stem
slides.notes: A sphere resting on three fixed balls always has its center at the same point in space, whatever direction its stem points. That is what lets the robot's own multi-orientation routine find the sphere's center as its tool center point, which deck 2 describes. The nest is simple to make: a steel base with three pockets, the balls pressed in, and holes to bolt it down. Its position matters only in that the robot must be able to seat the sphere from several directions. The dimensioned shop drawings are in appendix D of the stage-1 procedure, and as PNG files in docs/procedures/drawings/ of the repository: SC1-01 and SC1-02 adapter plates, SC1-03 and SC1-04 stems with the sphere interfaces, SC1-05 board adapter, SC1-06 nest base.

slides.title: Checks before the fixtures go to the robot cell
checklist: Adapter plates, stems, board adapter and nest base made to drawings SC1-01 to SC1-06
Adapter thread square to its stem-side face within 0.02 mm over 100 mm
Each stem straight: check against the straightedge
Both spheres matte, uniform and free of highlights
Each sphere diameter measured by micrometer after finishing, spread within 0.02 mm, temperature recorded
Board flat to 0.05 mm after painting and mounting
Each fixture weighed for its tool load data; witness marks across each stem-adapter joint
slides.notes: These are the build checks of sections 1 and 3a of the procedure, gathered in one place. Each one protects something the software cannot repair later: a crooked or bending stem moves the sphere center away from the measured tool center point, a shiny spot gives bad reads, and an unmeasured diameter or a bowed board puts a wrong reference into every observation. The fixture weights feed the robot's tool load data, which its absolute accuracy depends on. The dimensioned shop drawings are in appendix D of the stage-1 procedure, and as PNG files in docs/procedures/drawings/ of the repository: SC1-01 and SC1-02 adapter plates, SC1-03 and SC1-04 stems with the sphere interfaces, SC1-05 board adapter, SC1-06 nest base.
